# Shadow-implementation gate — build-time check that the contract is sufficient

2026-09-20. `src/openswe_traces/gate/shadow.py`, `scripts/shadow_gate.py`. Status: validation in progress.

## The check

For each unit, a second, independent implementation of the excised behaviour — the
*shadow* — is generated by a deliberately weak model whose only context is:

1. `contract.md` (else `instruction.md`), verbatim;
2. the declaration surface of every package holding an excised stub — all top-level
   decls, bodies of non-excised functions replaced by `{ /* body omitted */ }`;
3. exported-decl digests (same body elision) of the module-internal packages those
   files import.

`build_context` asserts no test file, nothing under `tests/`, no gold/cheat patch, and
no packaging metadata contributes a byte; the per-unit manifest (source + sha256) is
logged to `outputs/shadow_gate/contexts/`. The shadow is spliced over the
`panic("excised: …")` stubs, baked into the unit's own image (`environment/Dockerfile`),
and scored by the unit's own verifier (`tests/test.sh`), exactly as a solver patch is
scored. Gate verdict:

- **shadow passes** → the contract carries enough information to reconstruct the
  behaviour. That is the property trials were buying (~2.18M tokens each).
- **shadow fails** → either the contract is incomplete/wrong (it did not convey what
  the suite requires) or the suite is over-specified (it demands something only gold
  can produce). The failing assertion names the defect.

This is the generalisation of B10: instead of a regex for one unsatisfiable shape, it
detects every assertion only gold can satisfy. It is also the operational form of A13
("the contract must be consistent with gold"): rather than auditing prose against the
patch, we test whether the prose *reproduces the behaviour* the suite asserts.

## Weak model of record

`gemini-3.6-flash-minimal` via `cursor-agent` (`scripts/ops/ask_composer.py`,
credentials from `/home/evan/Documents/eval_tasks/.env`; every answer cached under
`outputs/composer_cache/`). Fallback `gpt-5.4-mini-low` on transport failure only.

`gpt-5.4-nano-low` was tried first and is **too weak**: on `helm-depresolver-L2` it
could not emit compilable Go even with the full signature surface — wrong arity on a
function whose signature was in context, unused imports, `repo.LoadIndexFile` called
on a string — through all three repair passes (two runs, both `fail_build`). A model
that cannot compile cannot separate good contracts from bad ones; the weakest model
that compiles is the right pick, and flash-minimal is that pick. Generation is
one-shot, temperature-default, ~40–90 s per call.

## Known trap fixed during bring-up

`MAX_DIGEST_CHARS` truncation cuts mid-file. At 60k it removed
`registry.Client.Pull` from depresolver's dep digest; the model then hallucinated
`DownloadChart` and fail_built. A missing signature is indistinguishable from a
capability failure, so caps now sit at 160k/240k — above the largest dep surface seen
(~80k for depresolver).

## Bring-up findings (v1 prompt, pre-fix)

Three defects surfaced in the first batch, none of them contract signals:

1. **ARG_MAX.** Prompts > ~128 KB cannot be a `cursor-agent` argv element —
   gin/kops dep surfaces overflowed it (`OSError: argument list too long`).
   `ask_composer.ask` now pipes the prompt on stdin.
2. **Mechanical compile failures dominated weak-model output:**
   - `_merge_imports` added every model-declared extra import into *every*
     excised file → `imported and not used` (gin-streamrenders, kops-taintparse).
   - Hallucinated import paths (`example.internal/chartkit/v4/internal/tlsutil`,
     `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` where go.mod has `go.yaml.in/yaml/v3`) → go tried to
     fetch them under `--network none`. Worse, `shadow.imports` was unioned
     across repair passes, so a phantom import from attempt 1 poisoned the
     apply of attempt 3 *which had it right* (helm-httpgetter).
   Fixes: imports merge only into files whose spliced code references the
   package (with `vN`/`yaml.v3` name-shape candidates); an import is merged
   only if the build can resolve it offline (stdlib-shaped, module-internal
   dir, or go.mod require/replace); imports come from the latest pass only.
   A dropped phantom becomes `undefined: pkg`, which the repair loop can act
   on; a fetch attempt is terminal.
3. **Base-image contamination (a third defect class, surfaced for free).**
   `helm-httpgetter-L2` fail_builds on
   `pkg/getter/httpgetter_test.go: module example.internal/chartkit/v4/...:
   network is unreachable`. That test file is **not** in the unit's src and
   **not** in the hidden suite — it is baked into `ladder-base:helm`'s `/app`
   from a different scrub (`chartkit/v4` module identity). `COPY src/ /app/`
   does not delete it, so `go test ./pkg/getter/` can never compile: the unit
   is unsolvable at every rung for *every* solver — which is exactly what the
   trial record shows (0/3 L0, 0/3 L2, 0/3* L5). A stale-file audit of the
   base images vs. each unit's src is now warranted; the gate flagged it
   without being asked.
4. **Model prior leaks on famous repos.** `helm-repindex-L2` PASSED the v1
   gate: the contract says "absolute URL used as-is" and "replaced, not
   duplicated" while the hidden `TestRIContractTable` asserts gold's
   join-basename + append for all shapes. The shadow reproduced gold anyway —
   flash-minimal has memorised helm's `index.go`. The gate measures
   contract+prior, not contract alone; on famous repos prior is large.
   Mitigation added to the prompt: *"Where your prior knowledge of this
   library disagrees with the contract, the contract wins."* (v2 prompt —
   it did NOT flip repindex: instructions do not subtract memorisation.)
   If a unit still passes on prior alone, that is a real limitation to
   report — the gate cannot fully subtract memorisation.

## Splice mechanics fixed during bring-up (v2/v3)

A shadow that cannot compile produces no signal, and the first two batches
were dominated by mechanical failures that had nothing to do with contracts.
Each fix below was driven by a named unit's failure; all are covered by unit
tests in `tests/test_shadow_gate.py`:

- **Reference-scoped, resolvable imports.** Model-declared imports merge only
  into files whose spliced code references the package, and only when the
  path resolves offline (stdlib-shaped, a module-internal dir, or a go.mod
  require/replace). Imports come from the latest repair pass, not a union —
  a phantom path from attempt 1 no longer poisons attempt 3.
- **Stdlib auto-imports.** `sha256.Sum256` without `crypto/sha256` is the
  most common weak-model omission; `STDLIB_IMPORTS` adds the import only
  when the identifier is referenced, unshadowed, and its name is not already
  bound (a forked `text/template` already owns `template`).
- **Name-aware rebind.** A file's existing `_ "crypto/rand"` is rebound to
  `crypto_rand "crypto/rand"` when the code needs that name (kops-issuecert);
  two blank imports sharing a base name yield the name to the deepest path
  only (kops-templater: `pkg/apis/kops` beats module root `kops`).
- **Helper decls.** `type`/`var`/`const` decls the model emits are appended
  with helper funcs (helm-repindex-L2rc5 needed `rawIndexFile`), skipping
  names that would redeclare. Import resolution re-runs after helpers land
  (a helper's `regexp.MustCompile` can need a package nothing else did).

| | actually defective (10 double-failure units) | actually good (10 flips + repindex-L2rc5 = 11) |

Precision 7/9 = 78%, recall 7/10 = 70%, accuracy 16/21 = 76%.
Model pass rate: 9/21 = 43%.

## Interpreting the misses

**The 3 "false negatives" are not all the same kind.**

- `helm-repindex-L2` is a true model-prior leak: the contract says an
  absolute URL is used as-is while the hidden `TestRIContractTable` asserts
  gold's join-basename behaviour for every shape — and the shadow passed
  anyway. flash-minimal has memorised helm's `index.go`; the "contract wins"
  prompt clause did not subtract it. On famous repos the gate measures
  contract+prior, and prior can carry a defective contract through.
- `gin-negotiate-L2` and `helm-chartrepo-L2` are different: their original
  L2 contracts (verified by manifest sha — `067ac70a`, `9dfb6f64`) are
  exhaustively detailed — byte-level match algorithm, dispatch table, error
  shapes, worked examples covering every hidden assertion. A weak model
  reconstructed the behaviour in one request. The plausible reading is that
  these contracts were *sufficient all along* and the 0/3 solver trials
  failed for solver-side reasons — "double-failure" conflates contract
  defects with solver failures, which is exactly the entanglement this gate
  exists to break. Counted as misses against the trial-derived labels; as
  measurements of contract sufficiency they may be correct.

**The 2 false positives are weak-model gaps, not contract defects.**
`helm-repindex-L2rc5` failing on `TestRIGet`/`TestRIIndexDirectory` is at
least consistent with its 2/3 trial record (the round-5 contract was still
imperfect). `kops-addonparse-L2` fails on property tests over edge cases —
flash-minimal missed details a stronger implementer would get.

**fail_build is the weak verdict.** Six of the seven correct flags are
fail_build, not fail_assert — "could not compile" is contract signal only
under the weak-implementer assumption, and it conflates contract gaps with
model capability. `helm-httpgetter` is the exception where fail_build named
a real defect (base-image contamination). The gate should report
fail_build and fail_assert separately, as it does — consumers should weight
fail_assert higher.

## Does it separate?

Yes, imperfectly — and well beyond the static linter it replaces (whose best
heuristics were 40% precise against a 39% base rate). The gate's required
calls all landed: `helm-depresolver` fails on the digest assertion by name
(`TestDRHashReqStable`), the round-5 repindex contract improvement shows up
as *different* failing assertions than the original's defect, and it
surfaced a base-image defect no check was looking for. Its failure modes are
named and bounded: prior-memorisation on famous repos (false negatives),
weak-model edge-case misses (false positives), and capability-vs-contract
entanglement in fail_build. As a pre-trial screen that halves wasted trials
at ~2% of trial cost, it clears the bar; as a verdict it should ship with
the per-unit outcome taxonomy intact.

## Cost and projected savings

- Per unit: ~53k est tokens, ~2.1 requests, ~4 min (cached gens make
  re-gates after splice fixes nearly free).
- Versus the ~2.18M-token solver trial it replaces: **~41× cheaper per unit**.
- If the gate flags even a third of the bank's defective units before
  trials, expected saving is ~0.3 × 2.18M ≈ 650k tokens per flagged unit at
  ~53k gate cost — order-of-magnitude win even at 70% recall.

Token figures are `(prompt+completion)/4` scale estimates — `cursor-agent`
does not report usage. Request counts are exact.

## Reproduce

```bash
# single units
uv run python scripts/shadow_gate.py UNIT_DIR [UNIT_DIR ...] --workers 3

# a whole sweep dir
uv run python scripts/shadow_gate.py --batch experiments/dose_response/sweep_L2 --workers 3

# results append to outputs/shadow_gate/results.jsonl (error outcomes are
# transient and retried); generations cached in outputs/shadow_gate/gen/
# and outputs/composer_cache/; contexts in outputs/shadow_gate/contexts/
```

Log: `outputs/SHADOW.log`. Model of record: `gemini-3.6-flash-minimal`.
